newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton rates seen falling in India, Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Cotton rates seen falling in India, Pakistan.

text.p: Cotton are likely to fall both in India and Pakistan on increased crop arrivals in the next few days, traders said on Thursday.
In India, Punjab cotton ruled weak on reports of increased crop arrivals while Gujarat varieties rose on the domestic market last week, traders said.
Traders in Bombay said export deals during the week remained low with players cautious after U.S. missile attacks on Iraq.
Some few thousand bales (170 kg each) were traded for export at 58/60 cents per pound, they said.
"Gujarat cotton attracted mill buying and lower than expected rainfall dragged prices upwards," one dealer said. Inflows were low as the 1995/96 (Sept-Aug) season drew to a close.
"Punjab cotton slid on reports of rising new crop arrivals and opening of forward trade on a discount compared to spot prices," said another dealer.
"Low rates for forward delivery prompted offering in spot delivery as far as Punjab cotton is concerned," a broker said.

In spot deals Bengal-deshi fell from 860/890 to 825/850 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) while October delivery was quoted at 820/825 rupees per maund. Punjab saw-ginned (spot delivery) fell by 10 rupees to 1,675/1,690 per maund, while October delivery was available at 1,640/1,650 per maund.
"New crop arrivals in Punjab will pick up in the coming days," one trader said.

Gujarat cotton remained firm during the week. In spot deals Gujarat Kalyan (medium-staple) rose by 400/600 rupees to 12,500/12,800 per candy (355.56 kg), while wagad cotton moved up by 700 rupees to 11,100/11,200 per candy.
"Overall market sentiment remained subdued lately on reports that state-owned agencies are planning to reduce selling prices to reduce stocks piled with them," one miller said.
"Last week some of these agencies have already reduced prices by 1,000/1,500 rupees per candy," he added.
In Pakistan, the rates were likely to fall sharply on increased crop arrival at ginning factories from farms, broker Haider Ali at the private Karachi Cotton Association (KCA) said.
The rates closed mixed on Thursday, partly owing to reports of damage to the crop by floods, he said.

The rates may fall below 2,000 rupees per maund because the 1996/97 crop is better than last year's, exporter Maqbool Sadi said. It could yield between 10.05 and 11 million 375-lb bales compared to 9.94 million bales in 1995/96.
But Omer Farooq Ehsan Chhani, vice-chairman of the Pakistan Cotton Ginners Association, said the production could reach 12.5 million bales.
In the kerb market, the rate for the 1996/97 NIAB-78 variety closed steady at 2,350 rupees per maund plus 10 percent sales tax, Ali said.
The KCA said exports had reached 1.82 million bales by August 25 since the 1995/96 season began on September 1, 1995.
